title: Jeremiah 36:20–32
context: The princes report the words to King Jehoiakim, who has the scroll brought and read to him in the winter house beside a fire (36:20–22). As Jehudi reads three or four columns at a time, the king cuts them off with a penknife and throws them into the fire until the whole scroll is consumed (36:23). The narrator notes that the king and his servants were not afraid and did not tear their garments, and that Elnathan, Delaiah, and Gemariah urged him not to burn it, but he would not listen (36:24–25). He orders the arrest of Baruch and Jeremiah, “but the LORD hid them” (36:26). The LORD tells Jeremiah to write the former words on another scroll and announces judgment on Jehoiakim: he will have no one to sit on David’s throne, and his dead body will be cast out to the heat by day and the frost by night (36:27–31; compare 22:19). 2 Kings 24:6 says that Jehoiakim “slept with his fathers” and that his son Jehoiachin reigned in his place, and this page names those accounts without forcing them together. Jeremiah gives another scroll to Baruch, who writes all the former words, “and many similar words were added to them” (36:32). Both traditions read the unit as shared ground: a king can burn a scroll, but he cannot destroy the word of the LORD.

verses.text: They went in to the king into the court, but they had laid up the scroll in the room of Elishama the scribe. Then they told all the words in the hearing of the king.
verses.arminianNotes: The princes leave the scroll in Elishama’s room and tell the king the words. Arminian readers note their caution. They report the message but keep the scroll away at first.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the princes acting carefully. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as narrative detail, and neither speculates about their motives beyond what the text says.

verses.text: So the king sent Jehudi to get the scroll, and he took it out of the room of Elishama the scribe. Jehudi read it in the hearing of the king, and in the hearing of all the princes who stood beside the king.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehudi reads the scroll in the hearing of the king and the princes. Arminian readers note that the king hears the word directly. He is given the same opportunity to respond as the people and the princes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the word brought before the king himself. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as setting up the king’s response, which is the climax of the chapter.

verses.text: Now the king was sitting in the winter house in the ninth month, and there was a fire in the brazier burning before him.
verses.arminianNotes: The king sits in the winter house, with a fire burning in the brazier. Arminian readers note the vivid setting. The detail of the fire prepares for what the king will do with the scroll.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the narrator’s careful scene-setting. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as historical detail, and neither presses it beyond the narrative purpose of preparing for 36:23.

verses.text: When Jehudi had read three or four columns, the king cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was in the brazier, until all the scroll was consumed in the fire that was in the brazier.
verses.arminianNotes: The king cut the scroll with a penknife and threw it into the fire until all was consumed. Arminian readers note the deliberate, repeated act of rejection. The king refuses the word column by column.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a vivid picture of contempt for God’s word. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing Jehoiakim’s rejection of the word, and both see in it a warning against refusing what God has spoken.

verses.text: The king and his servants who heard all these words were not afraid, and didn’t tear their garments.
verses.arminianNotes: The king and his servants “were not afraid, and didn’t tear their garments.” Arminian readers note the absence of repentance. Unlike the princes, they show no fear at the word of judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a hardened response. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as contrasting the king’s indifference with the princes’ fear (36:16), and many readers also contrast it with Josiah’s response to the book of the law (2 Kings 22:11).

verses.text: Moreover Elnathan and Delaiah and Gemariah had made intercession to the king that he would not burn the scroll; but he would not listen to them.
verses.arminianNotes: Elnathan, Delaiah, and Gemariah urged the king not to burn the scroll, but he would not listen. Arminian readers note that the king rejected counsel as well as the word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the king refusing both the word and those who pleaded for it. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that some officials sought to preserve the scroll, and that the king’s refusal was deliberate.

verses.text: The king commanded Jerahmeel the king’s son, and Seraiah the son of Azriel, and Shelemiah the son of Abdeel, to arrest Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet; but the LORD hid them.
verses.arminianNotes: The king orders the arrest of Baruch and Jeremiah, “but the LORD hid them.” Arminian readers note the LORD’s protection of his messengers. The king’s power cannot stop God from preserving them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s providential care for his servants. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that the LORD protects those who carry his word, and both note that the text does not say how they were hidden.

verses.text: Then the LORD’s word came to Jeremiah, after the king had burned the scroll, and the words which Baruch wrote at the mouth of Jeremiah, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s word came to Jeremiah after the king burned the scroll. Arminian readers note that the LORD speaks again. The king’s act does not silence him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s word continuing despite the king’s rejection. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as introducing the LORD’s answer to the burning of the scroll.

verses.text: “Take again another scroll, and write in it all the former words that were in the first scroll, which Jehoiakim the king of Judah has burned.
verses.arminianNotes: “Take again another scroll, and write in it all the former words.” Arminian readers note the endurance of the word. What was burned is written again, showing that God’s message cannot be destroyed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the word preserved by God’s command. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing the enduring nature of God’s word, which survives human attempts to destroy it.

verses.text: Concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah you shall say, ‘The LORD says: “You have burned this scroll, saying, ‘Why have you written therein, saying, “The king of Babylon will certainly come and destroy this land, and will cause to cease from there man and animal”?’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Jehoiakim burned the scroll, objecting to the warning that Babylon would come. Arminian readers note that the king’s anger was aimed at the content. He rejected the message of judgment itself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the king’s rejection of the LORD’s warning. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that Jehoiakim’s act was a refusal of the word, not merely of the scroll.

verses.text: Therefore the LORD says concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah: “He will have no one to sit on David’s throne. His dead body will be cast out in the day to the heat, and in the night to the frost.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehoiakim will have no one on David’s throne, and his body will be cast out to the heat and frost. Arminian readers report this soberly, compare 22:19, and note that 2 Kings 24:6 is not forced into agreement with it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the verse soberly as a word of judgment and hold questions about its relation to 2 Kings 24:6 with care. Shared ground: both traditions read it alongside 22:19 without dwelling on its details or forcing a harmony.

verses.text: I will punish him, his offspring, and his servants for their iniquity. I will bring on them, on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and on the men of Judah, all the evil that I have pronounced against them, but they didn’t listen.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: “I will punish him, his offspring, and his servants for their iniquity.” Arminian readers note that the judgment reaches those who shared in the king’s rejection, because “they didn’t listen.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see judgment on a people who refused to hear. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly as the consequence of not listening, and both see it as connected to the many warnings the people had been given.

verses.text: Then Jeremiah took another scroll, and gave it to Baruch the scribe, the son of Neriah, who wrote therein from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the book which Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire; and many similar words were added to them.
verses.arminianNotes: Baruch wrote again all the words, “and many similar words were added to them.” Arminian readers note that the word not only survives but grows. The king’s attempt to destroy it ends with a fuller scroll.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the endurance of God’s word, which no king can destroy. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a fitting close: the word of the LORD outlasts its opponents, and the faithful scribe continues his work.
